lead: Sampling turns a continuous signal into numbers taken at fixed instants, which is what PCM speech, digital storage and software radio need. If the samples are close enough, the signal can be rebuilt exactly. If they are too far apart, high frequencies fold down and pose as low ones, and no later filter can undo it. This chapter states the theorem, computes aliases, and covers ideal and flat-top reconstruction.
prereq: You need: the Fourier transform and band-pass spectra (see Fourier transform review and band-pass signals). Pulse modulation follows in PAM, PWM and PPM.

sections.h3: The theorem and the sample rate

blocks.text: A lowpass signal m(t) is bandlimited to fm hertz when its spectrum M(f) is zero for |f| > fm. The sampling theorem: such a signal is fixed completely by its samples m(nTs) if the sampling rate fs = 1/Ts ≥ 2fm. The lowest allowed rate 2fm is the Nyquist rate (samples/s); the largest spacing 1/(2fm) is the Nyquist interval (seconds).

Ideal sampling multiplies m(t) by an impulse train Σ δ(t − nT<sub>s</sub>). That train is periodic, so its spectrum is an impulse train f<sub>s</sub> Σ δ(f − kf<sub>s</sub>). Multiplication in time is convolution in frequency, so every spectral impulse places a copy of M(f) at kf<sub>s</sub>:

blocks.where: S(f) is the spectrum of the sampled signal s(t) = Σ m(nT<sub>s</sub>) δ(t − nT<sub>s</sub>); k runs over all integers. The copies are f<sub>s</sub> apart and scaled by f<sub>s</sub>.

blocks.text: The copy at 0 ends at fm; the copy at fs starts at fs − fm. They stay apart when fs ≥ 2fm, which is the theorem, and the gap fs − 2fm is the guard band. A lowpass filter with gain Ts (to cancel the factor fs) and any cutoff from fm to fs − fm keeps only the copy at 0 and returns m(t). At exactly 2fm the guard band is zero and a tone at fm can be sampled at its zero crossings, so real systems sample faster.

A tone at f0 above fs/2 does not vanish. Its samples equal those of a lower tone, the alias, at fa = |f0 − kfs|, with the integer k chosen so that 0 ≤ fa ≤ fs/2. The spectrum folds about fs/2, the folding frequency.

With f<sub>s</sub> = 7 kHz, a 1 kHz tone stays at 1 kHz, but a 4 kHz tone is above 3.5 kHz and folds to |4 − 7| = 3 kHz. The figure shows both views: a 4 kHz and a 3 kHz cosine through the same samples, and the spectral lines of the sampled signal. A 3.5 kHz reconstruction filter passes 1 and 3 kHz, so a 3 kHz tone that was never sent comes out.

So aliasing is stopped before the sampler. An anti-aliasing filter passes 0 to fm. A component at f folds to fs − f, which lands inside the message band when f ≥ fs − fm, so the filter must reach its stopband by fs − fm. The guard band is the room a real filter has to roll off; telephone speech uses fm = 3.4 kHz with fs = 8 kHz for this reason.

Ideal reconstruction is sinc interpolation: m(t) = Σ m(nTs) sinc((t − nTs)/Ts), with sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx). Each sinc pulse is 1 at its own instant and 0 at every other sample instant, so the sum passes through every sample. It needs an ideal lowpass filter, which real circuits only approach.

In natural sampling the pulse top follows m(t); in flat-top sampling a sample-and-hold keeps the top at m(nTs) for a width τ ≤ Ts. Holding filters the spectrum by H(f) = τ sinc(fτ), which droops the top of the message band: the aperture effect. A zero-order hold in a DAC is the worst case, τ = Ts. A shorter τ or a 1/sinc equalizer reduces it.

A band-pass signal of bandwidth B = f<sub>H</sub> − f<sub>L</sub> can be sampled below 2f<sub>H</sub> if the shifted copies interleave. When f<sub>H</sub> is a whole multiple of B, f<sub>s</sub> = 2B works; receivers use this to digitise an IF band directly.

examples.question: m(t) = 3 cos(2π·1000t) + 2 cos(2π·4000t) volts is sampled at f<sub>s</sub> = 7000 samples/s and passed through an ideal reconstruction filter with cutoff f<sub>s</sub>/2. Find the Nyquist rate, decide whether aliasing occurs, and list the output frequencies.
steps: f<sub>m</sub> = 4000 Hz, so the Nyquist rate is 2 × 4000 = 8000 samples/s (Nyquist interval 125 µs).
7000 < 8000 samples/s, so aliasing occurs. Folding frequency f<sub>s</sub>/2 = 3500 Hz.
Sampled spectrum: 1 kHz gives lines at 1, 7 − 1 = 6, 7 + 1 = 8 kHz, …; 4 kHz gives 4, 7 − 4 = 3, 7 + 4 = 11 and 14 − 4 = 10 kHz, ….
The 3500 Hz filter keeps 1 kHz and 3 kHz only.
Check at n = 1: 2 cos(2π·4/7) = 2 cos(3.590) = −1.802 V and 2 cos(2π·3/7) = 2 cos(2.693) = −1.802 V, the same sample.
examples.answer: Nyquist rate 8000 samples/s; aliasing occurs; the output is 3 cos(2π·1000t) plus a false 2 cos(2π·3000t).

examples.question: Speech bandlimited to 3.4 kHz is sampled at 8 kHz and rebuilt by a zero-order hold. (a) Find the guard band and the stopband edge of the anti-aliasing filter. (b) Where does a 10.5 kHz interferer appear? (c) Find the hold loss at 3.4 kHz.
steps: Guard band = f<sub>s</sub> − 2f<sub>m</sub> = 8000 − 6800 = 1200 Hz. Stopband edge = f<sub>s</sub> − f<sub>m</sub> = 8000 − 3400 = 4600 Hz.
Interferer: f<sub>a</sub> = |10 500 − 8000| = 2500 Hz, inside 0 to 4000 Hz and inside the speech band.
examples.answer: Guard band 1.2 kHz, stopband by 4.6 kHz; the interferer appears at 2.5 kHz; the hold loses 2.75 dB at 3.4 kHz, which a 1/sinc equalizer restores.

traps: f<sub>s</sub> = 2f<sub>m</sub> is the limit, not a design value: it leaves no guard band and can miss a tone at f<sub>m</sub>.
The alias must lie in 0 to f<sub>s</sub>/2. For 18 kHz at 8 kHz one subtraction (10 kHz) is not enough; two give 2 kHz.
Do not swap the Nyquist rate 2f<sub>m</sub> (samples/s), the Nyquist interval 1/(2f<sub>m</sub>) (s) and the folding frequency f<sub>s</sub>/2 (Hz).
The aperture effect is a droop of the wanted band by sinc(fτ), not aliasing; it shrinks with τ, while aliasing depends only on f<sub>s</sub>.

quiz.q: State the lowpass sampling theorem and define f<sub>m</sub>, f<sub>s</sub> and T<sub>s</sub>.
quiz.a: A signal bandlimited to f<sub>m</sub> Hz is fixed by samples taken at f<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2f<sub>m</sub> samples/s. f<sub>m</sub> is the highest message frequency, f<sub>s</sub> the sampling rate, T<sub>s</sub> = 1/f<sub>s</sub> the sampling interval.

quiz.q: Why is the anti-aliasing filter placed before the sampler, not after it?
quiz.a: After sampling, a folded component sits at the same frequency as real message content, so no filter can separate them. Before sampling, the filter removes whatever would fold into the band.

quiz.q: A 2.5 kHz tone is sampled at 4 kHz. Find the alias.
quiz.a: f<sub>s</sub>/2 = 2 kHz < 2.5 kHz, so f<sub>a</sub> = |2.5 − 4| = 1.5 kHz.

quiz.q: A 9 kHz tone is sampled at 8 kHz. Show that the samples are those of a 1 kHz tone.
quiz.a: cos(2π·9000n/8000) = cos(2πn + 2π·1000n/8000) = cos(2π·1000n/8000), since adding 2πn changes nothing. So every sample equals a 1 kHz sample, and 1 kHz lies inside 0 to 4 kHz.

quiz.q: Why does flat-top sampling cause the aperture effect, and how is it reduced?
quiz.a: Holding each sample for τ filters the spectrum by τ sinc(fτ), which droops the high message frequencies. A smaller τ pushes the sinc nulls out; a 1/sinc equalizer cancels the rest.

quiz.q: m(t) = 5 cos(2π·600t) + 2 cos(2π·1800t) is sampled at 3000 samples/s. Give the Nyquist rate and the output frequencies of a 1500 Hz reconstruction filter.
quiz.a: Nyquist rate = 2 × 1800 = 3600 samples/s > 3000 samples/s, so aliasing occurs. 600 Hz stays; 1800 Hz folds to |1800 − 3000| = 1200 Hz. Output: 600 Hz and 1200 Hz.

beyond: Not for the exam. Software-defined radios sample close to the antenna and choose a band-pass rate that drops the wanted channel near DC. Audio converters oversample by 64 or more and filter digitally, so the analog anti-aliasing filter can be simple. Search next for decimation filters and aperture jitter.
